issues.legal_issue: Rateable value calculated by reference to reasonable annual rent is limited by the standard rent under applicable rent-control legislation when the municipal law does not provide an independent valuation method or override that limit.
material_facts: The property was assessed for municipal property taxes under a municipal law that calculated rateable value by reference to the annual rent for which the land or building might reasonably be expected to let.

The municipal law did not define rateable value in specific terms or provide a detailed independent method for determining it, and it contained no overriding clause displacing the rent-control legislation.
The Corporation proposed to value land made available for construction by reference to its market value.
issues.conclusion: The rateable value was limited by the standard rent determined or determinable under the applicable rent-control legislation; market value alone could not displace that limit.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 154(1) of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act, the reasonable annual letting value must be read with the Bombay Rent Act, including Sections 5(10)(b) and 7. A rent-control limit constrains reasonable letting value unless the municipal law supplies a specific independent valuation method or an overriding provision. The Court relied on East India Commercial Co. (P) Ltd. v. Corporation of Calcutta, India Automobiles (1960) Ltd. v. Calcutta Municipal Corporation, Corporation of Calcutta v. Padma Debi, Guntur Municipal Council v. Guntur Town Rate Payers’ Association, Dewan Daulat Rai Kapoor v. New Delhi Municipal Committee, and Srikant Kashinath Jituri v. Corporation of the City of Belgaum; it distinguished legislation of the kind considered in Griha Yajamanule Samkhya.

rule.if: municipal_property_tax_assessment and valuation_uses_reasonable_annual_rent and rent_control_limits_chargeable_rent and not municipal_law_has_independent_valuation_method and not municipal_law_overrides_rent_control

predicates.municipal_property_tax_assessment: A municipal authority assesses land or a building for property tax.
predicates.valuation_uses_reasonable_annual_rent: The applicable valuation system measures the property by the rent for which it might reasonably be expected to let.
predicates.rent_control_limits_chargeable_rent: A rent-control system limits the rent that may lawfully be charged for the property.
predicates.municipal_law_has_independent_valuation_: The municipal law provides a specific, independent method for determining the property's rateable value.
predicates.municipal_law_overrides_rent_control: The municipal law expressly displaces the applicable rent-control limit.

issues.definition: When a municipal tax assessment uses reasonable annual rent and rent control limits lawful rent, the rateable value is capped by standard rent if the municipal law provides neither an independent valuation method nor an override.

issues.legal_issue: Rent-control restrictions inform the reasonable letting value even when the assessed premises have never previously been let or are occupied by their owner.
material_facts: The Corporation argued that the rent-control restrictions did not apply because the premises had never been let.
The Court considered the hypothetical rent a tenant would offer and held that the tenant would take applicable rent-control restrictions into account.
The Court also noted that the same valuation approach must apply to premises occupied by their owner.
issues.conclusion: The absence of a prior letting did not make the rent-control restrictions irrelevant to determining rateable value.
issues.legal_principle: Section 154(1) of the Bombay Municipal Corporation Act asks what rent the property might reasonably be expected to command. The Court held that the hypothetical tenant would consider the restrictions imposed by the Bombay Rent Act, including Section 7, even if the premises had not previously been let; otherwise owner-occupied premises could escape property taxation. The Court rejected the argument based on Section 6 of the Bombay Rent Act.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_assessment: A municipal authority assesses premises for property tax.
predicates.premises_never_previously_let: The premises have not previously been let to a tenant.
predicates.valuation_uses_hypothetical_tenant: The assessment determines reasonable letting value by considering what a hypothetical tenant would offer.

issues.definition: If premises never previously let are assessed by reference to a hypothetical tenant, applicable rent-control restrictions still inform the reasonable rental value.

issues.legal_issue: Demolition of a building and the resulting increase in the land’s building potential do not by themselves qualify as a ground for revising standard rent based on structural alteration or changed amenities.
material_facts: The owner demolished existing structures on part of its land and began construction of a new building complex.
The Corporation argued that demolition and the increased building potential justified revising the standard rent.
The Court described the relevant rent-revision ground as concerning structural alteration or changed amenities involving further capital investment by the owner.
issues.conclusion: Demolition of the building and increased building potential were not a ground under the relevant rent-revision provision for modifying standard rent.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11(a) of the Bombay Rent Act permits modification of standard rent in the specified circumstances involving structural alteration or a change in amenities with further capital investment by the owner. The Court held that demolition of a building was not such a circumstance.

predicates.rent_controlled_property_valuation_proce: A proceeding concerns valuation of property subject to rent-control restrictions.
predicates.existing_building_demolished: The owner demolished a building that previously stood on the property.
predicates.land_building_potential_increased: The property's potential for construction increased after the demolition.

issues.definition: In a rent-controlled property valuation proceeding, demolition and increased building potential alone do not justify revising standard rent.

issues.legal_issue: An assessee who objects to a municipal rateable-value assessment bears the burden of proving the applicable standard rent relied on to challenge the assessment.
material_facts: The assessee objected to the revised assessments but produced no material establishing the standard rent for the vacant land, the land under construction, or the completed building.
The assessee also did not disclose the amounts paid by occupants of the completed building until the Corporation obtained information after issuing a notice.
The Court accepted that the burden of proving the relevant standard rent rested on the assessee objecting to the assessment.
issues.conclusion: The burden of proving the standard rent was on the assessee objecting to the Corporation’s assessment.
issues.legal_principle: The assessee challenging the rateable value must establish the facts supporting the claimed standard-rent limit. The Court relied on the burden principle discussed in Assistant General Manager, Central Bank of India v. Commissioner, Municipal Corporation, and referred to National and Grindlays Bank Ltd. v. Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay concerning the Corporation’s assessment practice.

predicates.municipal_property_tax_assessment_challe: An assessee challenges a municipal authority's property-tax assessment.
predicates.assessee_claims_standard_rent_limit: The assessee relies on a standard-rent limit to dispute the assessed value.

issues.definition: When an assessee challenges a municipal property-tax assessment by relying on a standard-rent limit, the assessee must prove the applicable standard rent.

issues.legal_issue: Where the standard-rent limit governs the assessment but the parties have not focused on or produced evidence of the applicable standard rent, the assessment dispute may be remitted to allow the assessee to produce that evidence.
material_facts: The Court held that standard rent limited rateable value but found no evidence establishing the standard rent for the relevant land or buildings.
The parties and the lower courts had focused on the effect of an earlier decision about demolished buildings rather than on establishing standard rent.
The Court considered that the assessee should have an opportunity to discharge its burden because the core issue had not been properly addressed.
issues.conclusion: The Court set aside the lower-court judgments and restored the complaints to the Assessor and Collector for reconsideration after giving the assessee an opportunity to produce material supporting its objections.
issues.legal_principle: The assessee bears the burden of proving the standard rent that limits rateable value, but where the core issue was not adequately focused on and relevant material was not produced, the interests of justice may require remitting the assessment proceedings to permit that evidence to be presented.

rule.if: municipal_assessment_appeal and standard_rent_limits_rateable_value and standard_rent_evidence_missing and core_issue_not_focused_on

predicates.municipal_assessment_appeal: An appeal concerns a municipal property-tax assessment.
predicates.standard_rent_limits_rateable_value: The governing valuation rule limits rateable value by standard rent.
predicates.standard_rent_evidence_missing: The record contains no adequate evidence establishing the applicable standard rent.
predicates.core_issue_not_focused_on: The parties and decision-makers did not adequately focus on determining the applicable standard rent.

issues.definition: When a municipal assessment appeal is governed by a standard-rent limit but the evidence is missing because the issue was not adequately focused on, the assessment proceedings are remitted to allow evidence to be produced.
